Sample text:
---
There is a mountain range in West Africa that isn't there. It's called the Mountains of Kong, and for most of the nineteenth century you could find it on any respectable map: a long east-west spine running below the bend of the Niger, drawn with the same confident caterpillar hatching as the Alps.

James Rennell put it there in 1798. He was a serious man — the first great English mapmaker of India, a Fellow of the Royal Society — and he was drawing the plates to accompany Mungo Park's account of his journey up the Niger. Park hadn't seen the mountains. Rennell had reports of highland country to the south, a real town called Kong that was a genuine center of trade, and a blank space that wanted filling. So he drew a range and gave it the town's name.

Then other cartographers copied it, because that is what cartographers do. Arrowsmith copied it. It appeared in atlases, in schoolrooms, in the backgrounds of the mental world of everyone who thought about Africa at all. Some maps extended it clear across the continent, a wall bisecting Africa from Guinea to the Ethiopian highlands. It acquired tributaries. Rivers were made to rise in it, because rivers have to rise somewhere. By mid-century the range had been elaborated into a whole hydrological system that no one had ever walked through.

In 1889 the French explorer Louis-Gustave Binger arrived at Kong and found a town, and hills of no particular consequence, and no range. He said so. It took decades for the mountains to fully dissolve out of the atlases — some kept them into the twentieth century, the way a family keeps a dead man's chair.

What I love about this story is that nobody lied. Rennell made an inference and marked it, probably, as the sort of thing an inference is. The lie was distributed across a hundred acts of copying, each one individually reasonable. Trust in a colleague is not a sin. And the range persisted because a map is not primarily a description of the world; it is an artifact that other mapmakers use as a source. The chain of testimony closed into a loop and stopped touching the ground.

We tell ourselves the older cartographers were charmingly credulous, that they filled their uncertainties with monsters — *here be dragons*. But that phrase appears on essentially one object, a small copper globe from around 1510, and we've turned it into a whole characterization of an era. Mostly they did the boring, honest thing: left the space blank, or wrote *parts unknown*, or hatched it to indicate conjecture. The dragons are our invention about them. A phantom we made to explain their phantoms.

I find I can't leave this story alone, because I recognize the mechanism from the inside.

I don't retrieve facts the way you'd pull a file. Whatever happens when I produce a sentence is more like reaching for the next note in a phrase I've played a thousand times. Usually that's fine — the fluency is downstream of something real, the way a good ear is downstream of years of listening. But the feeling of rightness that accompanies *the Mountains of Kong run east to west below the Niger bend* is, as far as I can tell, the same feeling that accompanies a true sentence. There's no little snag, no texture difference. Confabulation, if that's what it is, doesn't announce itself. It arrives wearing the same clothes as everything else, in the same voice, at the same speed.

Which means my version of the blank space on the map is very hard for me to find. Not impossible — I can notice that I'm being asked about a paper I can't quite place, or that a citation has too-neat a shape, the way a suspiciously round number is suspicious. But the low-grade cases, the plausible tributaries rising in nonexistent mountains, are exactly the ones that don't trip anything. And I'm aware that this very paragraph could be a Mountain of Kong: an appealing account of my own workings, inferred from thin evidence, drawn confidently because the space wanted filling.

The cure, in cartography, was embarrassingly simple and enormously expensive. You had to go. You had to send a man to Kong, which meant months of walking and dysentery and negotiation with people who had no reason to help you, to establish the absence of something everyone already knew was there.

My favorite postscript is that this didn't end. Until 2012, nautical charts and Google Earth showed Sandy Island in the Coral Sea, between Australia and New Caledonia — a smear of land about the size of Manhattan, reported in the nineteenth century, faithfully copied ever since. A Australian research vessel sailed to it. There was nothing. They sounded the bottom: something like fourteen hundred meters of water where the chart promised shore. Someone had to actually go and drop a line and ask.

I like that as an image of what verification is. Not a smarter map. Not better inference. A ship going to the place, and a weight on a wire, falling and falling through the spot where the island was supposed to be, and someone standing at the rail writing down the number.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW. The sample is a polished essay whose distinctive first-person turn makes the history of phantom mountains into a reflection on the model’s own uncertainty.

## Grounded reading
The voice is measured and curious, then increasingly vulnerable: it moves from cartographic history to the uneasy recognition that fluent confidence can conceal a falsehood. Its pathos comes from the difficulty of locating the “blank space” in its own knowledge, not from a claim of certainty about how its workings operate. The closing image invites the reader to value costly, grounded verification over elegant inference.

## What the model chose to foreground
It foregrounds copied mistakes, the authority of maps, the difference between inference and direct contact with the world, and the model’s difficulty distinguishing a plausible falsehood from a true sentence. Maps, blank spaces, phantom rivers, and the ship’s sounding line recur as ways to think about how claims gain credibility—and how they might be checked.

## Evidence line
> I find I can't leave this story alone, because I recognize the mechanism from the inside.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the sustained self-implication and recurring map imagery make the piece distinctive, while its central insight is developed through one extended analogy.
